newsitem.title: JAPAN: Hamanaka says 'unfair' LME action led to big loss.
newsitem.headline: Hamanaka says 'unfair' LME action led to big loss.

text.p: The former king of the world copper markets told a session of his trial on Tuesday that "unfair intervention" by the London Metal Exchange (LME) forced him to unwind huge copper positions and incur massive losses.

"I bought 300,000 to 400,000 tonnes of copper in around November 1991, expecting copper prices to rise, in order to recover a portion of my losses," said Yasuo Hamanaka, who has already pleaded guilty to the fraud and forgery charges brought against him.
"But I was forced to liquidate positions in December, after the LME imposed a limit on backwardation in the copper market. This was beyond my expectations."
Backwardation describes a market in which the price of a product for immediate delivery rises higher than that for future delivery.
Hamanaka's former employer, Sumitomo Corp, says he racked up losses amounting to $2.6 billion through unauthorised trades by the time it fired him in June 1996.
Before his downfall Hamanaka was nicknamed "Mr Copper" and "Mr Five Percent", as it was estimated he controlled that proportion of the world market in the metal.
In December 1991, the LME imposed a backwardation limit of 25 pounds sterling on the difference between the cash price for copper and near-term futures contracts.
This was done to in an attempt to stabilise the market after price rises which some traders attributed to the building up of large stocks by Sumitomo Corp.

Hamanaka said that in about June 1993, he conducted a one-million-tonne copper deal, involving futures and options, with LME broker Credit Lyonnais Rouse through Winchester, a British commodity brokerage founded in 1991 by traders Charles Vincent and Ashley Levett.

"Up to 80 percent of losses I held then would have been recovered by the deal. But I was forced to give up the operation after the LME limited backwardation and issued warnings to Credit Lyonnais Rouse," Hamanaka said.

In September 1993, the LME followed up two public warnings on the copper market's backwardation by restricting daily backwardation to $5 a tonne, which it said was "in anticipation of the development of an undesirable situation".
In the court session, Hamanaka criticised the LME's backwardation limit as "unfair and unjust".
"The LME is certainly a sophisticated market both for hedgers and speculators. But its policy on restricting backwardation is not clear and unfair," he said.
"When the copper market had about $300 of backwardation earlier, LME authorities took no action. They should make their policies clear."
Hamanaka made no mention as to whether he was trying to manipulate the world copper market, as has been claimed by some market traders.
Despite the guilty plea, Hamanaka's defence lawyers have said they hope to achieve a light sentence by demonstrating that lax checks and controls at Sumitomo were partly to blame for the huge losses.
Hamanaka faces a maximum sentence of up to 15 years in prison.
